\section{The scaling calculus}\label{sec:calc}

\begin{lemma}[Propagation]\label{lem:prop}
If $V$ has diminishing returns from $a$ and $k\ge a$, then $\Delta(k+j)\le\Delta(k)$ for
all $j\ge0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induction on $j$, using $\Delta(k+j+1)\le\Delta(k+j)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Tangent cap]\label{lem:cap}
If $V$ has diminishing returns from $a$ and $k\ge a$, then
$V(k+j)\le V(k)+j\,\Delta(k)$ for all $j\ge0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$V(k+j+1)=V(k+j)+\Delta(k+j)\le V(k)+j\Delta(k)+\Delta(k)$ by induction and
Lemma~\ref{lem:prop}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zero}
If $V$ compounds then $V(0)\le0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$2V(0)\le V(0)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Secant floor]\label{lem:floor}
If $V$ compounds then $(m+1)V(b)\le V((m+1)b)$ for all $b,m\in\N$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Induction: $V((m+2)b)\ge V((m+1)b)+V(b)\ge(m+2)V(b)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Compounding Horizon]\label{thm:horizon}
If $V$ compounds and has diminishing returns from $a$, then for all $k\ge a$ and all
$b\in\N$,
\[ V(b)\le b\,\Delta(k). \]
Hence every marginal gain from $a$ on is at least $\sup_{b\ge1}V(b)/b$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For $b=0$ use Lemma~\ref{lem:zero}. Let $b\ge1$ and suppose $c:=V(b)-b\Delta(k)>0$. Pick
$N\in\N$ with $Nc>V(k)-k\Delta(k)$ and set $M=k+N$, so $(M+1)b>k$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:floor}, $(M+1)V(b)\le V((M+1)b)$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cap} with
$j=(M+1)b-k$, $V((M+1)b)\le V(k)+((M+1)b-k)\Delta(k)$. Hence
$(M+1)c\le V(k)-k\Delta(k)<Nc\le(M+1)c$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Compounding pushes the curve up at average slope $V(b)/b$ along multiples of $b$.
Diminishing returns holds it under a line of slope $\Delta(k)$. The argument has the same
flavour as Fekete's lemma.

If $V$ compounds, has diminishing returns from $0$, and $V(0)=0$, then $V(k)=kV(1)$ for

incompatible.

\section{The factor-residue model}\label{sec:model}

Let $\Omega$ be a finite nonempty population with the uniform distribution, $L:\Omega\to

invertible. Write $I(L;f)$ for mutual information in bits and $H(L)$ for the label

partition of $\Omega$ into fibres of $f$. The views are: the \emph{product view} $PQ$;
the \emph{sum dial}, which adds $P+Q$ (the gap dial $P-Q$ is symmetric); and the
\emph{joint residue view} $\rho$, whose fibres are those of $(P,Q)$. Set
$\HV=I(L;\rho)-I(L;PQ)$, and let $\SH$ be the conditional gain of the sum dial over the
product view. Then $0\le\SH\le\HV\le H(L)$.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{factor-residue hint curve} is $W(0)=0$, $W(1)=\SH$, $W(k)=\HV$ for $k\ge2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Third-hint saturation]
For any $h:R\times R\to\beta$,
$I(L;(\rho,h(P,Q)))=I(L;\rho)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Both views have the same fibres.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}
$W$ is monotone, has diminishing returns from $1$, and satisfies $W(k)\le H(L)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Compounding iff zero]
$W$ compounds if and only if $W\equiv0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:bounded}, $W\le0$, while monotonicity gives $W\ge W(0)=0$.
\end{proof}

Since $2$ is invertible, $(P+Q,PQ)$ determines $\{P,Q\}$ as the roots of

the orientation from the difference $P-Q$, and we use the following chain-rule bound.

\begin{proposition}[Sign-selector ceiling]
For any sign selector $s:R\to F$, $\HV\le\SH+\log_2|F|$.
\end{proposition}

Over $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$ with $p$ an odd prime, $|F|=2$: this is the one-orientation-bit
law. Over $\prod_{i<k}\mathbb Z/p_i\mathbb Z$ the coordinatewise selectors give

\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[One bit per field]
Over $\prod_{i<k}\mathbb Z/p_i\mathbb Z$ with odd primes $p_i$, $\HV-\SH\le k$.
\end{theorem}

\section{Discussion and future work}

On its window the curve does compound and its last gain does diminish. As a law, the
verdict contradicts itself, and the contradiction appears at the next measurement with a
margin of $0.91$ bits. The data alone cannot decide which half to drop. Boundedness by an
entropy rules out compounding, and in the residue model diminishing returns is forced. We
propose the replacement verdict \emph{hints compound locally, saturate globally}. The
positive third gain and the jump larger than one bit both point beyond a single prime field
and its residues.

Open directions: (1) an inflection bound $k^*\le\lceil B/\Delta(0)\rceil$ for bounded
curves with unimodal gains; (2) exactness of the $k$-field ceiling, attained by products
of orientation batteries; (3) a construction of extra-residue third hints, for instance a
second modulus combined through the Chinese remainder theorem; (4) quantitative,
finite-horizon versions of the Compounding Horizon Theorem.

<details><summary>Definitions: compounding and diminishing returns</summary>

* **Marginal gain:** $\Delta(k) = V(k+1)-V(k)$.
* **Compounding** ([superadditivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superadditivity)): $V(m)+V(n)\le V(m+n)$ for all $m,n$.
* **Diminishing returns from $a$:** $\Delta(k+1)\le\Delta(k)$ for all $k\ge a$. For $a=0$ this is discrete [concavity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concave_function).
</details>

{{visualization:0}}

The gains go $0.52 \to 1.91 \to 0.76$: **up, then down**. The curve is S-shaped, like a [logistic curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logistic_function), and not concave. The most the slogan can claim is diminishing returns from the second hint on.

## 2. Try it: the squeeze at the fourth hint

Move the slider for a hypothetical fourth measurement $V(4)$. Compounding requires $V(4)\ge V(2)+V(2)=4.86$. Diminishing returns requires $V(4)\le V(3)+0.76=3.95$. Try to find a value that satisfies both.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

No value works. The window is empty by $0.91$ bits, which is far more than measurement noise. You can also change $V(1),V(2),V(3)$ and see which datasets *would* allow the slogan to survive one more step.

## 3. Why: the Compounding Horizon Theorem

The squeeze at $k=4$ is a symptom of a general theorem.

> **Compounding Horizon Theorem.** If $V$ compounds and has diminishing returns from $a$, then for every $b$ and every $k\ge a$,
> $$V(b)\le b\,\Delta(k).$$
> Every marginal gain from $a$ on is at least every average rate $V(b)/b$ the curve has ever reached.

Two forces are at work. **Compounding copies**: $V(mb)\ge m\,V(b)$, so the curve climbs at least at slope $V(b)/b$ along multiples of $b$. **Diminishing returns caps**: $V(k+j)\le V(k)+j\,\Delta(k)$, so the curve stays under its tangent. If the copying slope were the steeper of the two, the copies would eventually rise above the cap.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details><summary>Proof of the Compounding Horizon Theorem</summary>

If $b=0$, compounding gives $2V(0)\le V(0)$, so $V(0)\le 0$. For $b\ge 1$, suppose $c=V(b)-b\Delta(k)>0$. Pick $N$ with $Nc>V(k)-k\Delta(k)$ and let $M=k+N$. The secant floor gives $(M+1)V(b)\le V((M+1)b)$. The tangent cap, applied with $j=(M+1)b-k\ge 0$, gives $V((M+1)b)\le V(k)+((M+1)b-k)\Delta(k)$. Subtracting, $(M+1)c\le V(k)-k\Delta(k)<Nc\le(M+1)c$, a contradiction. The argument has the same flavour as [Fekete's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subadditivity#Sequences).
</details>

{{visualization:1}}

For the data, the best average rate is $V(2)/2=1.215$. If the curve compounds and its returns eventually diminish, then every later gain is at least $1.215$ bits. The observed third gain was $0.76$.

<details><summary>Corollary: compounding + concavity from the start = a straight line</summary>

If $V(0)=0$, $V$ compounds, and its gains never increase, the tangent cap at $0$ gives $V(k)\le kV(1)$ and copying gives $V(k)\ge kV(1)$. Hence $V(k)=kV(1)$. In particular, compounding and *strictly* diminishing returns can never coexist.
</details>

## 5. The data cannot choose, but information can

Each half of the slogan, taken alone, does extend forever. Continuing along the last tangent ($+0.76$ per hint) gives diminishing returns. Switching to $V(k)=k^2$ for $k\ge4$ gives a compounding curve. The checker below confirms both, and shows which property each continuation breaks.

What breaks the tie is that **information is bounded**. Hints about a label can never carry more than the label's [entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entropy_(information_theory)).

> **Bounded Collapse.** A compounding curve with $V(k)\le B$ for all $k$ satisfies $V(k)\le 0$ everywhere. More generally, a ceiling $ck+b$ implies $V(k)\le ck$.

<details><summary>Proof</summary>
If $V(a)-ca=e>0$, copying gives $(N+1)V(a)\le V((N+1)a)\le c(N+1)a+b$, so $(N+1)e\le b$. This fails once $N>b/e$.
</details>

So every information-bounded continuation of the data fails to compound. The slogan should become **"hints compound locally, saturate globally."**

## 6. Inside the experiment: residues, roots, and orientation bits

The hints come from residues of the factors modulo a prime. The *product view* sees $pq$, the *sum dial* also sees $p+q$, and the *joint view* sees $(p,q)$ itself. Three consequences follow:

1. **A third residue hint is worth exactly zero.** Once $(p,q)$ is known, anything computed from it adds no information. So the curve saturates, and a monotone, bounded, saturating curve compounds only if it is identically zero.
2. **One prime field, one bit.** The pair $(pq, p+q)$ fixes $\{p,q\}$ as the roots of $x^2-(p+q)x+pq$. Only the *orientation*, which root is which, is still unknown, and that is worth at most $1$ bit.
3. **$k$ fields, $k$ bits.** Over a product of $k$ odd prime fields each coordinate has its own orientation bit, so the jump is at most $k$ bits.

The observed jump of $1.91$ bits is impossible over one field and fits under two.

/-! ## 1. The abstract scaling calculus -/

section Calculus

variable (V : ℕ → ℝ)

/-- The **marginal gain** of the `(k+1)`-st hint. -/
def marginal (k : ℕ) : ℝ := V (k + 1) - V k

/-- **Compounding** hint values: the curve is superadditive. -/
def Compounding : Prop := ∀ m n : ℕ, V m + V n ≤ V (m + n)

/-- **Diminishing returns from `a` on**: marginal gains are non-increasing for `k ≥ a`. -/
def DiminishingFrom (a : ℕ) : Prop := ∀ k, a ≤ k → marginal V (k + 1) ≤ marginal V k

variable {V}

/-- Marginal gains past `k` are bounded by the marginal gain at `k`. -/
theorem marginal_le_of_diminishing {a k : ℕ} (hV : DiminishingFrom V a) (hk : a ≤ k) :
    ∀ j, marginal V (k + j) ≤ marginal V k := by
  intro j
  induction j with
  | zero => simp
  | succ j ih =>
    have := hV (k + j) (by omega)
    rw [← add_assoc]; linarith

/-- **Tangent cap.**  A diminishing curve lies under its tangent line at any `k ≥ a`. -/
theorem diminishing_linear_cap {a k : ℕ} (hV : DiminishingFrom V a) (hk : a ≤ k) :
    ∀ j : ℕ, V (k + j) ≤ V k + j * marginal V k := by
  intro j
  induction j with
  | zero => simp
  | succ j ih =>
    have h1 := marginal_le_of_diminishing hV hk j
    have h2 : V (k + (j + 1)) = V (k + j) + marginal V (k + j) := by
      simp only [marginal, ← add_assoc]; ring
    rw [h2]; push_cast; nlinarith

/-- A compounding curve has `V 0 ≤ 0`. -/
theorem compounding_zero_nonpos (hC : Compounding V) : V 0 ≤ 0 := by
  have := hC 0 0; simp at this; linarith

/-- **Secant floor.**  A compounding curve dominates the multiples of any of its values. -/
theorem compounding_succ_mul (hC : Compounding V) (b : ℕ) :
    ∀ m : ℕ, ((m : ℝ) + 1) * V b ≤ V ((m + 1) * b) := by
  intro m
  induction m with
  | zero => simp
  | succ m ih =>
    have h := hC ((m + 1) * b) b
    have he : (m + 1) * b + b = (m + 1 + 1) * b := by ring
    rw [he] at h
    push_cast; nlinarith

/-- **THE COMPOUNDING HORIZON.**  If `V` compounds and its marginal gains diminish from `a`
on, every marginal gain past `a` is at least any average rate `V b / b` of the curve. -/
theorem compounding_horizon {a k : ℕ} (hC : Compounding V) (hV : DiminishingFrom V a)
    (hk : a ≤ k) (b : ℕ) : V b ≤ b * marginal V k := by
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos b with rfl | hb
  · simpa using compounding_zero_nonpos hC
  by_contra hcon
  push_neg at hcon
  set c : ℝ := V b - b * marginal V k with hc
  have hcpos : 0 < c := by linarith
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := exists_nat_gt ((V k - k * marginal V k) / c)
  -- take `M = k + N` copies of `b`
  set M : ℕ := k + N with hM
  have hMb : k ≤ (M + 1) * b := by
    have : (M + 1) * 1 ≤ (M + 1) * b := Nat.mul_le_mul_left _ hb
    omega
  have hlow := compounding_succ_mul hC b M
  have hup := diminishing_linear_cap hV hk ((M + 1) * b - k)
  rw [Nat.add_sub_cancel' hMb] at hup
  have hcast : (((M + 1) * b - k : ℕ) : ℝ) = ((M : ℝ) + 1) * b - k := by
    rw [Nat.cast_sub hMb]; push_cast; ring
  rw [hcast] at hup
  have hkey : ((M : ℝ) + 1) * c ≤ V k - k * marginal V k := by
    rw [hc]; nlinarith
  have hNc : (V k - k * marginal V k) < N * c := by
    rwa [div_lt_iff₀ hcpos] at hN
  have hMN : (N : ℝ) ≤ (M : ℝ) + 1 := by
    rw [hM]; push_cast; linarith [(Nat.cast_nonneg k : (0 : ℝ) ≤ k)]
  nlinarith

/-- **Compounding + diminishing from the first hint = linear.** -/
theorem compounding_diminishing_linear (hC : Compounding V) (hV : DiminishingFrom V 0)
    (h0 : V 0 = 0) (k : ℕ) : V k = k * V 1 := by
  have hup := diminishing_linear_cap hV (le_refl 0) k
  simp only [zero_add, marginal, h0, sub_zero] at hup
  rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos k with rfl | hk
  · simp [h0]
  · obtain ⟨m, rfl⟩ : ∃ m, k = m + 1 := ⟨k - 1, by omega⟩
    have hlow := compounding_succ_mul hC 1 m
    simp only [mul_one] at hlow
    push_cast at hup ⊢
    linarith

/-- Under compounding with diminishing returns from the start, all marginal gains equal
`V 1`. -/
theorem compounding_diminishing_marginal_const (hC : Compounding V)
    (hV : DiminishingFrom V 0) (h0 : V 0 = 0) (k : ℕ) : marginal V k = V 1 := by
  rw [marginal, compounding_diminishing_linear hC hV h0 (k + 1),
    compounding_diminishing_linear hC hV h0 k]
  push_cast; ring

/-- **Compounding and strictly diminishing returns are incompatible.** -/
theorem no_strict_diminishing_of_compounding (hC : Compounding V)
    (hV : DiminishingFrom V 0) (h0 : V 0 = 0) (k : ℕ) :
    ¬ marginal V (k + 1) < marginal V k := by
  rw [compounding_diminishing_marginal_const hC hV h0,
    compounding_diminishing_marginal_const hC hV h0]
  exact lt_irrefl _

/-- **Affine ceilings collapse to linear ones under compounding.** -/
theorem compounding_affine_ceiling {c b : ℝ} (hC : Compounding V)
    (hceil : ∀ k : ℕ, V k ≤ c * k + b) (a : ℕ) : V a ≤ c * a := by
  by_contra hcon
  push_neg at hcon
  set e : ℝ := V a - c * a with he
  have hepos : 0 < e := by linarith
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := exists_nat_gt (b / e)
  have hlow := compounding_succ_mul hC a N
  have hup := hceil ((N + 1) * a)
  push_cast at hup
  have hkey : ((N : ℝ) + 1) * e ≤ b := by rw [he]; nlinarith
  have : b < N * e := by rwa [div_lt_iff₀ hepos] at hN
  nlinarith

/-- **Bounded curves cannot compound upwards.**  A compounding curve with any uniform ceiling
is nonpositive everywhere. -/
theorem compounding_bounded_nonpos {B : ℝ} (hC : Compounding V) (hB : ∀ k, V k ≤ B) (a : ℕ) :
    V a ≤ 0 := by
  have := compounding_affine_ceiling (c := 0) (b := B) hC (by simpa using hB) a
  simpa using this

end Calculus
